But the thought that sustained me when I began my work now only drives me deeper into despair. All my ideas and hopes have come to nothing. Like the archangel who wanted unlimited power, I am chained in an everlasting hell. My imagination was vivid, and I also had great powers of reasoning and concentration. Together, these abilities allowed me to conceive of making a man and to carry out that creation. Even now, I cannot calmly remember the dreams that filled me while my work was unfinished. In my thoughts I walked through heaven, sometimes rejoicing in my powers, sometimes burning with excitement at what they might achieve. Since childhood I had held great hopes and high ambitions. But how far I have fallen! Oh, my friend, had you known me then, you would not recognize the broken man before you. I rarely felt despair. I seemed to be carried forward toward a magnificent destiny, until I fell, never, never to rise again.”

Must I lose this remarkable man, then? I have longed for a friend, someone who would understand and love me. Here on these empty seas I have found him, yet I fear that I have gained him only to learn his worth and then lose him. I want to help him find happiness in life again, but he rejects the thought.

“Thank you, Walton,” he said, “for your kindness toward someone so miserable. But when you speak of new relationships and new loves, do you believe anyone could replace those I have lost? Could any man be what Clerval was to me, or any woman become another Elizabeth? Even when we do not love our childhood companions for any exceptional qualities, they have a hold on our hearts that later friends rarely gain. They know our childhood natures, which may change but are never entirely erased. They can therefore judge more confidently whether our actions come from honest motives. Unless dishonesty has appeared early, a sister or brother will never suspect the other of deceit. Yet another friend, however devoted, may find himself viewed with suspicion despite everything. My friends were dear to me not merely through long familiarity and shared experience, but for their own worth. Wherever I go, Elizabeth's comforting voice and Clerval's conversation will always whisper in my ears. They are dead, and in this loneliness only one feeling can persuade me to stay alive. If I were pursuing some great task or plan that promised widespread benefit to other people, I could live to complete it.

At the steps where we had brought him aboard, and throughout the journey since, I had watched carefully for any sign that we were under suspicion. I had seen nothing. No boat had accompanied or followed us earlier, and certainly none was doing so now. Had any boat kept alongside us, I would have headed for shore, forcing it either to continue ahead or to reveal its intentions. But we maintained our course without any sign of interference.

He wore his boat cloak and, as I have said, looked entirely at home in the scene. Remarkably—though perhaps his wretched life explained it—he was the least anxious among us. He was not indifferent: he told me he hoped to live long enough to see his gentleman become one of the finest gentlemen in a foreign country. Nor, as I understood him, was he inclined to passivity or resignation. He simply saw no reason to anticipate danger. When it arrived, he faced it, but he would not worry before then.

“If you knew, dear boy,” he told me, “what it means to sit here beside my dear boy and enjoy my smoke, after spending day after day inside four walls, you'd envy me. But you don't know what it's like.”

“I think I understand the pleasures of freedom,” I replied.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head solemnly. “But you don't understand them as I do. You'd have to have been locked up, dear boy, to know them as I do. But I'm not going to get gloomy.”

It struck me as inconsistent that any consuming idea could have led him to risk his freedom, and even his life. Then I considered that freedom without danger might be so far removed from everything he knew that it could never mean to him what it meant to another man. I was close to the truth, for after smoking a while he said:

“You see, dear boy, when I was over there, on the other side of the world, I was always looking toward this side. Life there felt flat, even though I was getting rich. Everyone knew Magwitch. Magwitch could come and go, and nobody would give him a thought. They aren't so easy about me here, dear boy—at least, they wouldn't be if they knew where I was.”

“If everything goes well,” I said, “in a few hours you'll be completely free and safe again.”

“Well,” he answered, taking a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And do you think so?”

At any rate, he believed so. Yet who could say? ... No. There had been nothing else. Vanity had prompted him to spare her. Hypocrisy had made him assume the appearance of goodness. Curiosity had led him to experiment with self-denial. He understood it now.

But the murder—must it pursue him throughout his life? Must his past weigh upon him for ever? Could he truly confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence against him remained. The portrait itself—that was proof. He would destroy it. Why had he preserved it all this time? Once he had delighted in seeing it alter and grow aged. Lately there had been no delight. It had robbed him of sleep at night. Whenever he was absent, he had trembled lest someone else should see it. It had cast sadness over his passions. The very recollection had spoiled many happy moments. It had served him as a conscience. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it.

Looking about him, he caught sight of the knife with which he had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had washed it repeatedly until not a stain remained. It shone, bright and gleaming. Having slain the painter, it would now slay the painter's work and everything the work signified. It would slay the past; once that was dead, he would be free. It would put an end to this monstrous life of the soul, and, released from its dreadful warnings, he would find peace. He snatched up the knife and drove it into the picture.

A scream rang out, followed by a crash. Its agony was so terrible that the terrified servants awoke and stole from their rooms. Two gentlemen passing through the square below halted and gazed up at the large house. They went on until they encountered a policeman, whom they brought back with them. He rang the bell repeatedly, but received no answer. Save for a light at an upper window, the whole house lay dark. Presently he withdrew to a neighbouring portico, where he stood watching.

“Whose residence is that, Constable?” inquired the older gentleman.

“Mr. Dorian Gray's, sir,” the policeman replied.

As they departed, the gentlemen exchanged a look and sneered. One was the uncle of Sir Henry Ashton.

Within the servants' quarters, the half-dressed domestics whispered together in subdued voices. Old Mrs. Leaf wept and twisted her hands. Francis was deathly pale.

When some fifteen minutes had passed, he summoned the coachman and a footman and crept up the stairs.
